text:
Scrap the Parking Mandates

Most cities in the English-speaking world have a rule that almost nobody voted for and almost nobody has read. It says that a new apartment must come with a set number of parking spaces, a restaurant with so many per table, a bowling alley with so many per lane. These minimum parking requirements sit deep in planning codes, and they have shaped our cities more than any grand plan ever did. Cities should remove them.

Start with where the numbers come from. Planners rarely measure the parking demand of the neighbourhood in front of them. They copy ratios from neighbouring towns or from handbooks built on small surveys of suburban sites where parking was free and no bus ran. The result has the look of engineering and the rigour of folklore. A requirement of one space per 200 square feet of shop floor is not a finding about your high street. It is a guess from somewhere else, enforced as law.

The guess is expensive. A space in a surface lot costs thousands of dollars to build once land is counted. A space in a structured garage commonly costs tens of thousands, and underground parking costs more still. That money does not vanish. It is folded into rents, into the price of a flat, into the cost of a meal. The tenant who cannot afford a car pays for a space she will never use. The shopper who walks subsidises the one who drives. Bundling parking into everything is a transfer from people who own fewer cars, who are on average poorer, to people who own more.

Mandates also stop housing from being built at all. On a small urban lot, the required spaces often will not physically fit alongside the homes, or they fit only with a garage that wrecks the project's finances. So the lot stays a lot. The buildings many people love most in older neighbourhoods, the corner shop with flats above, the three-storey walk-up, the terrace with no driveway, are illegal to build again in much of the city that contains them. Converting an empty office or an old warehouse into homes frequently fails for the same reason: the building predates the rules and has nowhere to put the cars.

Then there is the land itself. Parking takes space, and a city that requires a lot of it spreads out. Shops sit behind seas of asphalt, destinations drift apart, and walking between them becomes unpleasant or impossible. That makes driving necessary, which makes more parking seem necessary, and the code duly demands it. Mandates manufacture the demand they claim to be meeting. They also pave over ground that could absorb rain, shade a street, or pay property tax at a far higher rate per acre than a car park does.

The strongest objection is spillover. If a new building has too little parking, the argument runs, its residents will fill the surrounding streets, and existing neighbours will bear the cost. That concern is real, but it is a problem with how kerb space is managed, not a reason to regulate what happens on private land. Streets fill up because on-street parking is given away or priced far below its value. Cities have the tools to fix that directly: permits, meters, time limits, prices that vary with demand. Requiring every developer to build a garage in order to protect free kerbside parking is a costly, indirect way to solve a problem that a permit scheme solves cheaply.

The second objection is that people still drive, so parking is still needed. Of course it is. Removing a minimum is not imposing a maximum. It bans nothing. Developers still have to sell or let what they build, and lenders still ask whether a project will find tenants. Where buyers want parking, parking gets built, because homes without it would not sell. The difference is that the amount is decided by people with money at stake and knowledge of the site, rather than by a table in a zoning code.

This is no longer a theoretical argument. Buffalo dropped its requirements citywide in 2017. Minneapolis, Austin, San Jose and others have followed, and Oregon and California have curtailed mandates near transit. England abandoned national minimum standards years ago in favour of local discretion. The evidence so far is undramatic, which is the point. Developers in these places still build parking, usually somewhat less than the old rules demanded, and projects on awkward sites that were previously unbuildable have gone ahead. No city has descended into chaos.

Some places will need to pair the reform with better kerb management and decent accessible parking rules, which should remain. Those are details to get right, not reasons to delay.

Minimum parking requirements raise the cost of housing, waste urban land, lock in car dependence, and rest on numbers nobody can defend. Cities face a housing shortage and a climate problem, and here is a rule that makes both worse. Repealing it costs the public purse nothing. Few reforms offer so much for so little. Strike the mandates and let each building supply the parking it actually needs.
